article.title: Fighting ICE From the Ground Up
article.author: Guest Author
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. When immigration agents take a father from his workplace, the consequences extend far beyond the moment of arrest. His children may lose their primary caregiver. His family may suddenly face eviction or hunger. Relatives may spend days trying to determine where he has been taken, while struggling to raise money for an attorney, telephone calls, or food inside a detention facility. Those were among the experiences described at the October 2026 Left Coast Forum at Cal State LA, where grassroots organizers gathered for a panel titled The Impact of ICE Session I: How Communities Have Responded to ICE Raids and Where We Go From Here. MaryLinda Moss The discussion brought together three activists working on the front lines of Southern California's immigration enforcement crisis: Erika Schwerdt of Strength Based Community Change (SBCC), Jacqueline Méndez of Defend Migrants Alliance and International Migrants Alliance, and John Parker of the Harriet Tubman Center and Community Self-Defense Coalition. Moderated by MaryLinda Moss of NELA Alliance for Democracy and No Concentration Camps California, the session offered something more substantial than a catalog of abuses. It described an emerging infrastructure of community defense, built through cooperation among organizations that recognize they cannot confront federal enforcement alone. The Devastation That Follows an ICE Arrest Erika Schwerdt, who organizes primarily in the Antelope Valley, emphasized that immigration enforcement is particularly difficult to monitor in rural communities. Erika Schwerdt Unlike densely populated Los Angeles neighborhoods, where witnesses may quickly gather when agents appear, residents of sprawling desert communities often live miles apart. Families may not discover that someone has been detained until that person fails to return from work. Schwerdt described receiving desperate calls from relatives asking what to do when a father or aunt simply disappears. She cited ICE data indicating that more than 14,000 people had been detained or arrested in Los Angeles County during the period she examined, while volunteers in the LA Rapid Response Network had verified approximately 3,000 cases. The disparity, she explained, reflects the enormous challenges facing community-based monitoring efforts. But statistics tell only part of the story. Schwerdt recounted an incident in which agents allegedly dragged a man from his vehicle, beat him, and left his truck running on the roadway. When a roadside-assistance worker attempted to help the family recover the vehicle, she said, an agent threatened him with arrest. The family included elderly grandparents, one experiencing dementia, who struggled to comprehend what had happened. Other families face an equally devastating aftermath: children without parents, spouses suddenly deprived of income, and detainees attempting to survive on inadequate food while paying inflated prices for basic necessities. Schwerdt described receiving calls from detained people asking for commissary assistance and worrying about wives and children left behind. For these families, she stressed, the trauma does not end when the immediate crisis passes. Children may need years of emotional support. Relatives must assume unfamiliar caregiving responsibilities. Families struggling financially before an arrest can be pushed into outright destitution. This is why SBCC emphasizes community education, training rapid responders and legal observers, and building relationships that can provide practical assistance long after agents have departed. Schwerdt also warned that enforcement tactics have shifted toward less visible operations, including detentions associated with immigration check-ins and other routine encounters. The absence of dramatic television footage, she argued, should not be mistaken for an end to enforcement. From Detention to Collective Resistance Jacqueline Méndez described a complementary approach: organizing alongside detained migrants and their families rather than treating those affected as passive recipients of assistance. Jacqueline Méndez Through Defend Migrants Alliance and International Migrants Alliance, organizers have supported campaigns involving people held at the Adelanto detention facility, including detainees engaged in hunger strikes. One campaign centered on Luis, a detainee who helped lead a hunger strike. According to Méndez, his family and supporters organized legal, media, and community committees to publicize conditions and demand his release. Luis eventually gained his freedom and continued organizing through a group called Guerreros of Adelanto, connecting formerly detained people to support one another. The experience challenged a common portrayal of immigrants as powerless victims. "They are survivors, they are fighters," Méndez declared. Another campaign concerned Rafael, a Salvadoran asylum seeker whom Méndez said agents detained while he was preparing his family's pupusa stand in Pacoima. While confined at Adelanto, Rafael reportedly became an advocate for fellow detainees, drawing attention to serious medical problems, including allegations that people with diabetes had been denied necessary medication. His case helped inspire a broader campaign against what organizers call medical violence at Adelanto. Méndez emphasized that solidarity can take many forms. Families need funds, legal assistance, public attention, visits, and opportunities to communicate with the outside world. Even something as simple as writing a letter can make an enormous difference to someone confined in a detention center. Her message was straightforward: people need not wait until they become experienced activists to contribute. They can join existing organizations, support families, visit detainees where permitted, participate in campaigns, and help publicize the experiences of people whose lives have been disrupted. Building a Community Self-Defense Network John Parker, representing the Harriet Tubman Center and Community Self-Defense Coalition, described efforts to unite organizations across Los Angeles in coordinated opposition to immigration raids. John Parker The coalition, he said, encompasses approximately 85 organizations engaged in activities ranging from neighborhood patrols and political education to court solidarity and community outreach. An important part of the strategy involves establishing a visible presence in neighborhoods where residents fear immigration enforcement. Volunteers distribute information, explain legal rights, encourage residents to report suspected enforcement activity, and build relationships with churches and other trusted community institutions. For Parker, the objective is not simply to respond after someone has been detained. It is to build relationships that make residents less isolated and more capable of acting collectively. That work has become more difficult, he warned, as agents change their methods. Rather than conducting highly visible operations that attract crowds of protesters, enforcement teams may wait until someone leaves home or stops at a gas station. The coalition has responded by emphasizing neighborhood networks, public education, and communication among organizations. Parker also challenged local political leaders, arguing that opposition to federal immigration policies means little without meaningful accountability for local law enforcement. He criticized what he sees as inadequate resistance from Los Angeles political officials and urged activists to organize independently of politicians who offer rhetorical sympathy without corresponding action. His analysis placed immigration enforcement within a broader struggle over racial division and economic inequality. By portraying migrants as threats, Parker argued, political leaders can divide working-class communities that otherwise share many common interests. He invoked the historical cooperation of the Black Panthers, Brown Berets, and Young Lords as an example of the multiracial solidarity needed today. Who Profits From Detention? One of the discussion's most troubling themes concerned the financial incentives embedded in the immigration detention system. Panelists criticized the role of private detention corporations and contractors, arguing that incarceration has become a lucrative business whose revenues depend on keeping people confined. Schwerdt described the contradiction facing organizers who raise money so detainees can purchase basic necessities. Families and supporters must pay for expensive commissary items and telephone services, even while believing that these expenses help sustain the system they oppose. The problem is not abstract. Schwerdt explained how responding to calls from detained people can consume hours. Each conversation may begin with basic questions: Where are you being held? Do you have an attorney? What assistance does your family need? There may be another detainee waiting to use the telephone, and another after that. Eventually, the emotional burden becomes overwhelming even for experienced organizers. This reality underscored a recurring message throughout the panel: sustaining the work requires attention not only to the people directly harmed by detention but also to those supporting them. The Movement Must Belong to the People Despite the severity of the experiences described, the discussion was not simply an expression of despair. The panelists offered concrete examples of families organizing, detainees resisting abuse, volunteers learning new skills, and organizations setting aside differences to cooperate. They also insisted that affected communities must remain central to the movement. Schwerdt rejected competition over organizational recognition, declaring that the movement and its data do not belong to any individual organizer. Left Coast Forum Video Archive "The only people that can claim some of it are the people that are directly affected," she said. Méndez similarly called for more public storytelling to counter the portrayal of immigrants as criminals or statistics. A father, grandfather, artist, student, or worker should not be reduced to an arrest number. Moss closed by reminding participants that they must also care for themselves while confronting the trauma and devastation experienced by immigrant families. The panel's underlying lesson was that resistance cannot depend on occasional demonstrations alone. It requires durable networks capable of responding when a neighbor disappears, accompanying families through immigration proceedings, sustaining contact with detainees, challenging public officials, and rebuilding the bonds of solidarity that fear and repression seek to destroy. In Southern California, those networks are already taking shape. The question now is whether they can grow quickly enough—and broadly enough—to meet the challenges ahead.
